scenarios.title: Scenario 6 — Structured Data Extraction
scenarios.brief: An insurance broker extracts data from certificates of insurance sent by many carriers. Claude returns the insured name, carrier, policy number, limits, deductibles and dates through a tool with a JSON schema. A validator checks each result before it is posted to the broker's system.

questions.question: Many certificates do not show a deductible at all. In the schema, deductible is a required number. For these certificates, the extraction returns 0 or copies the coverage limit into the field. Those values are posted as if they were printed, and reviewers cannot tell them apart from real ones. What is the best fix?

options.t: Add two example certificates with no deductible to the prompt, each with its expected output.
options.why: Works, but only partly. Examples show what to do when no deductible is printed, but while the schema demands a number the model has no honest value to return.

options.t: Make deductible nullable in the schema, and state in its description when to return null.
options.why: Best. A required number forces the model to invent one. A nullable field gives it an honest way to say “not printed”.

options.t: Keep deductible required and have the model enter -1 whenever no deductible is printed.
options.why: Works, but fragile. -1 marks the gap, but it is still a number: every system downstream must know the convention, or -1 posts as a real value.

options.t: Add a deductible_printed flag beside the number, and have reviewers ignore the number when it is false.
options.why: Works, but the invented number stays. The flag tells reviewers to ignore it, but the required field still puts a made-up value in the record, where other systems can use it.

questions.decider: In the schema, deductible is a required number.
questions.explanation: Required fields push the model to invent values when the source lacks them. Optional or nullable fields, with a description of when to leave them empty, prevent that.

eli5.question: When a certificate has no deductible, the extraction makes one up (0, or the limit). The clue: the schema says the field must always hold a number.
eli5.answer: A form with a box that must contain a number, and no “not applicable” option, makes people write something, anything. Add “leave blank if not printed” and the made-up values stop. In a JSON schema that's a nullable field. Rule: the model invents values when the schema leaves it no honest answer. Make missing values nullable.
options: Showing examples doesn't help while the form still has no blank option.
Correct. Let the field be empty when nothing is printed.
-1 is still a number someone can mistake for a real one.
A “please ignore” sticker helps, but the made-up number is still on the form.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think made-up values are a prompting problem. Here the schema causes them: a required number has no valid way to say “not printed”, so the model fills it. Fix the schema first; examples help only once the schema allows an honest answer.
deep.diagram:
required number + nothing printed → model invents 0
nullable number + nothing printed → null (honest)

guide.obj: 4.3 Structured output via tool use and JSON schemas

questions.question: Each coverage line has a line_type enum with five values, such as general liability, auto and umbrella. Certificates now often list other lines, such as cyber or professional liability. The extraction forces these into the nearest listed value, so cyber often posts as general liability. Brokers need to know what each of these lines really is. Which schema change is the best fix?

options.t: Add cyber and professional liability to the enum, and add more values as carriers bring new lines.
options.why: Works, but delays the problem. The two new values fix today's lines, but the next new line type is forced into the nearest value again until someone changes the schema.

options.t: Make line_type nullable, and leave it empty when a line matches none of the listed values.
options.why: Works, but loses the answer. An empty value stops the wrong label, but brokers still cannot see what the line is, and the type was printed on the certificate.

options.t: Change line_type to a free-text string that holds the carrier's own wording.
options.why: Works, but drops the structure. Every line keeps its real name, but the common types now arrive spelled many ways, and reports that group by type break.

options.t: Add other to the enum, with a line_type_detail field for the carrier's wording.
options.why: Best. Known types stay clean enum values, and any new type lands in other with its real name kept beside it.

questions.decider: Brokers need to know what each of these lines really is.
questions.explanation: A closed enum forces unknown values into the nearest option. Add an other value plus a detail field so new categories are captured without losing the known ones.

eli5.question: A list of insurance types has five choices. New types like cyber get squeezed into the closest choice, so they post wrong. The clue: brokers need to know what each line really is.
eli5.answer: Think of a form with tick boxes for five fruits. Someone brings a mango and ticks “apple”. The usual fix is a sixth box, “other”, with a line to write “mango”. In a schema that's an enum with other plus a detail field. Rule: a list that keeps growing gets an “other” value and a field for the real name.
options: Adding boxes for today's new fruits works until next week's new fruit arrives.
Leaving the box blank stops the wrong tick, but nobody knows it was a mango.
Letting people write anything loses the neat tick boxes everyone counts by.
Correct. Keep the boxes, add “other”, and write the real name next to it.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a wrong category means the list is missing a value, so you add the value. That fixes today, but carriers keep inventing new lines. The schema needs a place for values nobody listed yet, while known values stay clean for reporting.
deep.diagram:
enum: gl | auto | wc | umbrella | property | other
  “Cyber Liability” → other + detail: “Cyber Liability”
  “Auto”            → auto

evidence.means: Keep the known values clean, which free text ([[2]]) gives up, and add an escape with detail: [[3]].

deep.rule: A category list that keeps growing gets an other value plus a detail field.

guide.obj: 4.3 Structured output via tool use and JSON schemas

questions.question: A validator rejects any policy whose expiry date is earlier than its effective date. On failure, the pipeline resends the certificate with the message “Validation failed, please retry.” Most retries fail the same way. In sampled failures, both dates are printed clearly, but the model has put each date in the other's field. Which change is the best fix?

options.t: Resend with the specific error: the two fields, the values returned and the rule they broke.
options.why: Best. Both dates are on the page, so the model can fix the mix-up once it is told exactly what went wrong.

options.t: Swap the two dates in code whenever the expiry date comes out earlier than the effective date.
options.why: Works, but hides the cause. It fixes this exact swap, but a date that was misread, not swapped, would also be flipped and posted as if correct.

options.t: Send each certificate that fails the date check to a person in the review queue.
options.why: Works, but gives up too early. A person will fix it, but the information is on the page and a clear retry fixes most of these without anyone's time.

options.t: Add example certificates to the prompt that show where several carriers print the two dates.
options.why: Works, but only usually. Examples may cut the first-pass swaps, but the retry still sends a vague message, so the failures that remain still repeat.

questions.decider: On failure, the pipeline resends the certificate with the message “Validation failed, please retry.”
questions.explanation: When the information is in the document, a retry works if it carries the specific validation error. A generic retry message gives the model nothing to correct.

eli5.question: When the dates come back swapped, the system just says “try again”, and the model makes the same mistake. The clue: the retry message says nothing about what was wrong.
eli5.answer: A teacher hands back homework marked only “wrong, redo it”. The pupil guesses and gets it wrong again. Write “you swapped the start and end dates” and it's fixed in one go. That is retry with the specific validation error. Rule: when the answer is on the page, retry with the exact error. When it isn't on the page, retrying won't help.
options: Correct. Tell the model exactly which fields broke which rule.
Quietly swapping in code fixes this case, but also “fixes” dates that were simply misread.
A person can fix it, but the model could have fixed it with a clear note.
Better examples help the first try, but the retry note is still useless.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think retries don't work, because most of them fail. They fail here because the message is vague. The guide's line is about where the information is: if it is in the document, a retry with the specific error fixes it; if it is absent, no retry can.
deep.diagram:
extract → validator: expiry < effective
  vague:    “Validation failed” → same swap again
  specific: “expiry 2026-01-01 < effective 2027-01-01,
             fields may be swapped” → fixed

evidence.means: The decider. The retry gives no detail, so the model has nothing to correct.

evidence.quote: Most retries fail the same way
evidence.means: Retrying itself is not the problem; the content of the retry is.

evidence.quote: both dates are printed clearly, but the model has put each date in the other's field
evidence.means: The information is on the page, so a retry can work. A person ([[2]]) isn't needed, and a code swap ([[1]]) would also flip misread dates.

evidence.quote: Which change is the best fix?
evidence.means: Fix the failing step, the retry: [[0]]. Examples ([[3]]) help the first pass only.

deep.rule: Information on the page but extracted wrong? Retry with the specific validation error.

guide.obj: 4.4 Validation, retry, and feedback loops for extraction quality
guide.quote: Retry-with-error-feedback: append specific validation errors on retry

questions.trap: More context or reasoning instead of structure
questions.question: Each schema field has a detailed description of what to extract. Accuracy is high on certificates that use the standard industry form. It drops on carriers' own policy schedules, which put limits in paragraphs, footnotes or tables with several columns. The prompt has instructions only, with no complete document worked through. What is the most effective way to raise accuracy on these schedules?

options.t: Add notes to each field description on where values sit in non-standard layouts.
options.why: Works, but more of the same. The descriptions are already detailed, and prose about layouts teaches less than seeing a few documents worked through.

options.t: Classify each document first, and send schedules to a separate prompt written only for them.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. A second prompt adds a classifier and another prompt to maintain, and it still has no worked examples.

options.t: Add three or four worked schedules in different layouts, showing where each limit is.
options.why: Best. Worked examples are the strongest way to show how to handle varied layouts, and the prompt has none yet.

options.t: Make the limit fields nullable and send schedules with empty limits to a reviewer.
options.why: Works, but different problem. It stops guessed limits from posting, but accuracy on schedules stays where it is and reviewers do the work.

questions.decider: The prompt has instructions only, with no complete document worked through.
questions.explanation: When detailed instructions still give uneven results across document layouts, a few worked examples covering those layouts are the most effective next step.

eli5.question: Claude does well on the standard form but badly on carriers' own layouts. The clue: the instructions are already detailed, and there are no worked examples at all.
eli5.answer: A new clerk reads a thick manual and still gets lost in an unusual invoice. Sit with them through three odd invoices, pointing at where each number is, and they get it. That's few-shot examples: a few documents worked through in the prompt. Rule: instructions already detailed but layouts vary? Add 2–4 worked examples of those layouts.
options: Adding more pages to the manual helps a little; the clerk already has plenty of words.
A separate manual for odd invoices is more work, and it still has no worked examples.
Correct. Show a few odd layouts worked through, step by step.
Leaving hard numbers blank for a person stops guesses, but doesn't make the clerk better.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think better instructions fix accuracy. Here the descriptions are already detailed. What is missing is examples: showing a few varied documents and where each value was found teaches layouts that prose cannot describe well.

Cause

Classify, then route to separate prompts

evidence.quote: Each schema field has a detailed description of what to extract
evidence.means: Instructions are already detailed, so more notes ([[0]]) add little.

evidence.quote: It drops on carriers' own policy schedules, which put limits in paragraphs, footnotes or tables with several columns
evidence.means: Same fields, varied layouts. The schema is fine, so a separate prompt ([[1]]) is more than needed.

evidence.quote: The prompt has instructions only, with no complete document worked through
evidence.means: The decider: the strongest tool for varied layouts is unused.

evidence.quote: What is the most effective way to raise accuracy on these schedules?
evidence.means: Raise accuracy, not route around it as [[3]] does: [[2]].

deep.rule: Detailed instructions but uneven results across layouts? Add a few worked examples of those layouts.

guide.obj: 4.2 Few-shot prompting for consistency and quality
guide.quote: Few-shot is the most effective technique for consistent, actionable output when instructions alone are inconsistent

questions.question: A schema change means the archive of past certificates must be extracted again, about 40,000 documents. The results are due at the end of next week. Each certificate needs one extraction call and no other tools. Brokers keep using the live pipeline for new certificates in the meantime. Which approach best fits this re-extraction?

options.t: Run the archive through the live pipeline at night, in chunks that leave room for daytime traffic.
options.why: Works, but full price. It finishes in time, but every call costs the normal rate and someone has to schedule and watch the chunks.

options.t: Submit the archive with the Message Batches API, one certificate per request, keyed by custom_id.
options.why: Best. Results are needed in days, not seconds, and each request is one call with no tools. Batches cost half as much, and custom_id matches each result to its certificate.

options.t: Have a coordinator spawn parallel extraction subagents across the archive, several per response.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. It is fast, but it adds an orchestration layer and pays full price for speed nobody needs this week.

options.t: Send the archive to the live API with ten certificates in each request to cut the number of calls.
options.why: Works, but crowds each request. Fewer calls, but full price, attention spread across ten documents, and one bad file spoils the rest of its request.

questions.decider: The results are due at the end of next week.
questions.explanation: Large, latency-tolerant jobs of single-call requests belong on the Message Batches API: half the cost, up to a 24-hour window, results matched by custom_id.

eli5.question: A big pile of old certificates must be redone, and the deadline is next week. The clue: nobody needs the answers right now, and each one is a single call.
eli5.answer: Posting 40,000 letters by express courier is fast and expensive. Bulk mail costs half and arrives within a day, which is fine when the deadline is next week. That bulk service is the Message Batches API, and the label on each envelope is the custom_id. Rule: not urgent and one call each → batch. Someone waiting → live.
options: Express courier at night works, but you still pay express prices.
Correct. Bulk mail: half the price, done within a day, each letter labelled.
A team of couriers running in parallel is quick, but costly and not needed this week.
Stuffing ten letters in one envelope saves stamps, but they get mixed up.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a big job needs the fastest setup. The deadline is a week away, so speed is worth nothing here and cost is what matters. The Batches API gives half the cost and returns within a day. Its limit, no multi-turn tool calls, does not bite: each certificate is one call.
deep.diagram:
40,000 requests, each custom_id = certificate ID
  → Message Batches API (≤ 24 h, 50% cost)
  → results matched back by custom_id

head: Situation
Right mechanism
Why
rows: Large job, results needed in days, one call each
Someone is waiting, such as a broker uploading now
Each document needs several tool-call turns
Batches don't support multi-turn tool calls
Large job due within the hour
No need to redo the rest

evidence.quote: about 40,000 documents
evidence.means: Large volume, so cost per call matters.

evidence.quote: The results are due at the end of next week
evidence.means: The decider. Days of slack, so paying full price for speed ([[2]], [[0]]) buys nothing.

evidence.quote: Each certificate needs one extraction call and no other tools
evidence.means: The Batches limit on multi-turn tool calls does not apply.

evidence.quote: Which approach best fits this re-extraction?
evidence.means: One document per request, matched by ID: [[1]]. Packing ten into one request ([[3]]) mixes documents.

deep.rule: Big, not urgent, one call per document → Message Batches API with custom_id.

guide.quote: Good for non-blocking/latency-tolerant (overnight reports, weekly audits)

questions.question: The extraction agent runs in a loop with two lookup tools. The loop ends when Claude's reply contains the phrase “EXTRACTION COMPLETE”. Sometimes Claude writes that phrase while also asking for a tool call, and the loop exits before the tool runs. Other runs never write the phrase and stop at the iteration cap. How should the loop decide when to stop?

options.t: Continue while stop_reason is tool_use, and end the loop when it is end_turn.
options.why: Best. The API reports on every response whether Claude wants a tool or has finished. That is the signal the loop is built on.

options.t: Keep the phrase, but run any requested tools first and stop on the next turn without a tool call.
options.why: Works, but still reads text. It fixes the early exit, but runs that never write the phrase still stop at the cap.

options.t: Have Claude return a status field, and stop when it says complete with no tool call pending.
options.why: Works, but reinvents the signal. A structured flag is sturdier than a phrase, but Claude can still forget it, and the API already reports this.

options.t: End the loop from a hook once every required schema field has a value.
options.why: Works, but wrong signal. It ends many runs on time, but fields can fill before the lookups are done, and runs with a missing field still hit the cap.

questions.decider: Sometimes Claude writes that phrase while also asking for a tool call, and the loop exits before the tool runs.
questions.explanation: An agent loop continues while stop_reason is tool_use and ends on end_turn. Parsing the reply text or using an iteration cap as the main stop are anti-patterns.

eli5.question: The loop stops when Claude writes a magic phrase. Sometimes it writes it too early, sometimes not at all. The clue: the loop is reading Claude's words to decide when the job is done.
eli5.answer: A waiter who waits for you to say “that's all” sometimes leaves while you're still ordering. Most restaurants just watch whether you've closed the menu. The API gives that closed menu on every reply: stop_reason. tool_use means “still ordering”; end_turn means “done”. Rule: stop the loop on stop_reason, not on words.
options: Correct. Watch the menu, not the words.
Better, but people who never say “that's all” still keep the waiter there all night.
A “done” card on the table is better than words, but the menu already tells you.
Leaving when the plates are full can be too early, or never happen.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the loop needs a clearer “done” message from Claude. But the API already says, on every response, whether Claude wants a tool (tool_use) or has finished (end_turn). Any signal Claude writes itself, a phrase or a flag, can be missing or early.
deep.diagram:
response → stop_reason?
  tool_use → run tool, append result, loop
  end_turn → stop
deep.mapTitle: How should an agent loop know it is done?

head: Approach
Problem
Verdict
rows: A phrase in the reply text
Claude can forget or misjudge it
Iteration cap as the main stop
Cuts off real work or runs long
Not the same as all work done

evidence.quote: The loop ends when Claude's reply contains the phrase
evidence.means: The loop reads text to decide termination, an anti-pattern.

evidence.quote: Sometimes Claude writes that phrase while also asking for a tool call, and the loop exits before the tool runs
evidence.means: The decider. The response was really tool_use; the loop ignored it.

evidence.quote: Other runs never write the phrase and stop at the iteration cap
evidence.means: Any self-written signal ([[1]], [[2]]) can go missing, and filled fields ([[3]]) can come before the work is done.

evidence.quote: How should the loop decide when to stop?
evidence.means: Use the API's own signal: [[0]].

deep.rule: Continue on tool_use, stop on end_turn. Never parse text or rely on a cap to stop.

guide.obj: 1.1 Design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution
guide.quote: Continue the loop when stop_reason == "tool_use"; terminate when "end_turn"

questions.question: Some submissions hold a broker's cover email plus several certificates. The coordinator reads the email, which names the client and the location each certificate covers. It then spawns one subagent per certificate with the task “Extract this certificate.” Subagents often assign certificates to the wrong location. Each subagent receives only its certificate. Which change is the best fix?

options.t: Give subagents a scoped get_cover_email tool, and tell them to call it before extracting.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. Each subagent can read the email itself, but that adds a tool and a call per certificate for facts the coordinator already has.

options.t: Have subagents return a location guess, and let the coordinator correct it against the email.
options.why: Works, but too late. The coordinator can catch wrong guesses, but it redoes the matching after the fact instead of giving subagents the answer up front.

options.t: Run one agent over the whole submission, email and certificates together, with no subagents.
options.why: Works, but gives up the split. One agent sees everything, but long submissions crowd one context and lose the parallel, focused extraction.

options.t: Add the client name and the location list from the email to each subagent's task prompt.
options.why: Best. Subagents see only what their prompt gives them. The coordinator already has these facts, so it passes them on.

questions.decider: Each subagent receives only its certificate.
questions.explanation: Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's context. Facts they need, which the coordinator already holds, must be written into each subagent's prompt.

eli5.question: The coordinator read the cover email, but the helpers it sends out only get one certificate each, so they guess the location wrong. The clue: each helper receives only its certificate.
eli5.answer: A manager reads the client's letter, then hands each temp a single page saying “file this”. The temps don't know which site each page belongs to. Write the client and site list on each handout and they file it right. That handout is the subagent's task prompt. Rule: subagents know only what you put in their prompt.
options: Letting each temp fetch the letter works, but it's extra trips for facts the manager already has.
Fixing the filing afterwards works, but it's checking work that could have been right first time.
One person doing everything works, but a big pile slows them down and mistakes creep in.
Correct. Write the facts on each handout.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think subagents know what the coordinator knows. They don't: a subagent starts with an empty context and sees only the prompt it is given. The coordinator already holds the facts, so the simplest fix is to pass them in.
deep.diagram:
coordinator: email → client, locations
  ├→ subagent 1: cert 1 + client + locations
  └→ subagent 2: cert 2 + client + locations

rows: Put them in the subagent's prompt
Subagent needs varied lookups nobody can predict
A scoped tool for that lookup
It can fetch what it finds it needs

Pass the complete findings in its prompt

Checking subagent output against known facts
A safety net, not the main fix

evidence.quote: The coordinator reads the email, which names the client and the location each certificate covers
evidence.means: The facts are already in the coordinator's hands, so a lookup tool ([[0]]) is extra machinery.

evidence.quote: It then spawns one subagent per certificate with the task “Extract this certificate.”
evidence.means: The task prompt carries no context.

evidence.quote: Each subagent receives only its certificate
evidence.means: The decider: the subagent has no way to know the locations.

evidence.quote: Which change is the best fix?
evidence.means: Pass the facts in: [[3]]. Correcting afterwards ([[1]]) is too late; dropping subagents ([[2]]) changes the design.

deep.rule: Subagents inherit nothing. Put the facts they need into their prompt.

guide.obj: 1.3 Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
guide.quote: Subagent context must be provided explicitly in the prompt

questions.question: The agent calls verify_carrier to check a carrier against the licensing registry, then post_certificate to send the result on. One session handles several certificates in turn. Sometimes the agent posts a certificate without verifying its carrier first. Compliance requires that no certificate from an unverified carrier is ever posted. Which change meets this requirement?

options.t: Make a verification ID from verify_carrier a required input of post_certificate.
options.why: Works, but checks shape, not fact. A required field makes skipping harder, but nothing confirms the ID belongs to this carrier or came from a real check.

options.t: Set tool_choice to force verify_carrier on each session's first request.
options.why: Works, but only once. It verifies the first carrier, but a session handles several certificates, and later ones can still skip the check.

options.t: Add a hook that blocks post_certificate until verify_carrier has passed for that carrier.
options.why: Best. Code checks every post, for every certificate in the session, and refuses any carrier that has not passed.

options.t: Add a system-prompt rule to verify each carrier first, with two examples of verify-then-post.
options.why: Works, but only usually. The rule and examples cut the skips, but prompt instructions still fail now and then, and compliance allows no misses.

questions.decider: Compliance requires that no certificate from an unverified carrier is ever posted.
questions.explanation: When a step must happen every time, enforce it in code: a hook or prerequisite gate that blocks the downstream tool until the check has passed for that item.

eli5.question: The agent should check each carrier before posting, but sometimes it skips the check. The clue: compliance says an unchecked carrier must not get through, not even once.
eli5.answer: A sign saying “show your ticket” stops most people. A turnstile that opens only for a valid ticket stops everyone. Here the turnstile is a hook on post_certificate that looks up whether this carrier passed. Rule: must happen every time → code gate. Usually is good enough → prompt.
options: Asking for a ticket number helps, but nobody checks the number is real.
Checking only the first person in a group lets the rest walk through.
Correct. A turnstile on every post, for every carrier.
A sign works most of the time, and the rule says most is not enough.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think forcing the tool or a required field is as strong as a hook. tool_choice forces one call on one request, and a session here posts several certificates. A required field checks that something was passed, not that the check happened for this carrier. Only code that runs on every post meets an absolute rule.
deep.diagram:
post_certificate(cert, carrier)
  → hook: verified[carrier]?
       yes → allow
       no  → block, tell agent to verify first
deep.mapTitle: A step must come before another. How strong must the control be?

Why

One call must come first in a single-item run
Nice to have, misses do no harm

evidence.quote: One session handles several certificates in turn
evidence.means: Forcing the first request ([[1]]) covers only the first certificate.

evidence.quote: Sometimes the agent posts a certificate without verifying its carrier first
evidence.means: The prompt-led order already fails sometimes; a stronger prompt ([[3]]) lowers the rate, not to zero.

evidence.quote: Compliance requires that no certificate from an unverified carrier is ever posted
evidence.means: The decider: zero misses, so enforcement must be in code.

evidence.quote: Which change meets this requirement?
evidence.means: A gate that checks this carrier on every post: [[2]]. A required ID ([[0]]) can be reused or made up.

deep.rule: Must happen every time → a hook or prerequisite gate in code, checked on every call.

questions.question: The team wants to send only doubtful fields to reviewers and post the rest directly. Accuracy was measured on a uniform random sample and is high overall. Scans from small carriers are rare in that sample. Compliance wants error rates measured for each document type before any field skips review. Which two steps together achieve this?

options.t: Label a new sample with a quota for each document type, including enough small-carrier scans.
options.why: Best. A quota per type gives enough examples of each, including the rare scans, to measure each type's error rate.

options.t: Label a larger uniform random sample, and report accuracy for each field across all documents.
options.why: Works, but rare types stay rare. A bigger sample and per-field numbers help, but small-carrier scans are still too few to measure, and results are not split by type.

options.t: Have the model report a confidence for each field, and send any field below a fixed cutoff to a reviewer.
options.why: Works, but unchecked. Field-level routing is the right shape, but self-reported confidence is not matched against real errors, so the cutoff is a guess.

options.t: Calibrate each field's confidence on the labelled set, and send fields below its threshold to review.
options.why: Best. Thresholds set from labelled results route each field by its measured error rate, which is the routing the team wants.

questions.decider: Compliance wants error rates measured for each document type before any field skips review.
questions.explanation: High overall accuracy can hide weak document types. Measure with a stratified sample, then route fields by confidence calibrated on that labelled set.

eli5.question: The team wants to skip review for fields the model is sure about. The clue: compliance wants each type of document measured, and rare scans barely appear in the sample.
eli5.answer: A school says “95% passed”, but only two pupils from the small village took the test. To know how the village does, you test a set number from each place. That's a stratified sample. Then you only trust a pupil's “I'm sure” once you've checked how often “sure” was right. That's calibrated confidence. Rule: measure each type on purpose, then route by confidence checked against real answers.
options: Correct. Test a set number from each type, rare ones included.
A bigger random test still has hardly any village pupils.
Trusting “I'm sure” without checking how often it's right is a guess.
Correct. Set each cut-off from how often “sure” was really right.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think high overall accuracy means it is safe to skip review. An average can hide a weak document type, and rare types barely show up in a uniform sample. Two things are needed: measure each type on purpose, and route each field by confidence that has been checked against labelled answers.

questions.question: Reviewers check flagged certificates against the source PDF. Policy schedules can run to dozens of pages. Most of each review is spent hunting for where a value was printed. The extraction output holds the values and nothing else. Which change most speeds up these reviews?

options.t: Return a calibrated confidence for each field, and open each review on the lowest-scoring ones.
options.why: Works, but different problem. It tells reviewers which fields to check first, but not where on the dozens of pages each value is.

options.t: Highlight every place in the PDF where each extracted value's text appears.
options.why: Works, but noisy. Exact matches help, but a date or limit can appear many times, and a misread value appears nowhere.

options.t: Return each value with the page number and the exact text span it was read from.
options.why: Best. Reviewers jump straight to the source of each value, which removes the hunting.

options.t: Return the values grouped under the schedule's own section headings, in document order.
options.why: Works, but only narrows it. Section headings point to the right area, but reviewers still search within each section.

questions.decider: Most of each review is spent hunting for where a value was printed.
questions.explanation: Keep the source with each extracted value: page and exact span. Reviewers then verify instead of search.

eli5.question: Reviewers spend most of their time looking for where each number came from in a long document. The clue: the output gives values but no sources.
eli5.answer: A student's essay quotes facts with no page numbers, so the teacher hunts through the book to check each one. Ask for “page 12, line 4” beside each fact and checking takes seconds. That's source provenance: each value carries the page and exact text it came from. Rule: if people check values against a document, return the location with each value.
options: Saying which facts are shaky helps choose what to check, not find it.
Highlighting every match helps, but common numbers light up everywhere, and misread ones nowhere.
Correct. Give the page and the exact words for each value.
Chapter titles narrow the search, but you still read the chapter.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think reviews are slow because there are too many fields, so you prioritise them. The stem says the time goes into finding each value. The fix is to keep the source with each value, the same way a research report keeps a source with each claim.
